correctness.rationale: For any nondegenerate d-simplex (\(d\ge3\)), independent barycentric gradients yield exactly V(1-q(z))_+^d as the overlap covariogram. The distribution is its Euclidean ball integral divided by V. The q support-function representation gives the sharp initial radius a=1/max||L||; expanding below a gives the exact polynomial. Up to the explicit smaller of the next-normal and pairwise-cap thresholds, only disjoint winning hyperplane caps contribute; integration yields the complete first branch. Substitution and dominated convergence yield the nonzero beta coefficient and exponent \((3d+1)/2\). The \(d=3\) integral and seven-normal geometry check algebraically. Directly executed independent polyhedral intersection tests and spherical radial quadrature for two tetrahedra, and cap checks for a four-simplex, agree. Finite checks are supplemental, not infinite proofs.

originality.rationale: The new assertion concerns the exact first Euclidean-radius departure of a simplex two-point distance law in every dimension at least 3, including its first full cap branch, its sharp exponent and multiplicity. Known homothetic simplex overlaps and general covariogram-distance identities supply premises but not this local Euclidean radial integration; triangle/polygon formulas only cover dimension 2. The closest published research claim about simplex two-point distances uses a Minkowski gauge, not Euclidean balls. The earlier parallelotope branch concerns a distinct polyhedral family. An unindexed equivalent in older stereology remains an authentic residual priority risk, not a known covering result. Beck (2023) establishes elementary formulas for all natural moments in arbitrary polyhedra, including tetrahedra; moment determinacy does not directly supply the exact first local CDF clipping branch.

value.rationale: The shape-dependent first Euclidean distance transition of a natural family of convex bodies is a meaningful geometric-probability invariant. The formula completely identifies its first critical radius and whole next regime for every simplex, explains the universal dimension-dependent singular exponent, includes the sharp normal multiplicity, and resolves tetrahedra via a finite list of seven natural face/edge separations. The precise boundary and first correction have mathematical significance beyond a routine recomputation of pair-distance moments.
